'''Seymour Sack''' (September 8, 1929 – November 29, 2011) was an American physicist and [[nuclear weapon design|nuclear weapons designer]] at [[Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory]]. Sack worked as a program manager and primary designer on the [[B77 nuclear bomb]] and the [[W84]] [[thermonuclear bomb|thermonuclear warheads]]. For his work on nuclear weapon design, he was awarded the [[Ernest Orlando Lawrence Award|E. O. Lawrence Award]] in 1973 (currently awarded by the U.S. [[Department of Energy]]) and the presidential [[Enrico Fermi Award]] in 2003 for lifetime achievement in the field of nuclear energy.

==Early life and education==
Sack was born on September 8, 1929, in [[New York City]].<ref name="Lucchetti2011">{{cite web |last=Lucchetti |first=Linda A. |title=LLNL mourns the loss of Seymour Sack |website=Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory |date=2011-11-30 |url=https://www.llnl.gov/article/37506/llnl-mourns-loss-seymour-sack |access-date=2026-05-10}}</ref><ref name="Grover2018">{{cite report |last1=Grover |first1=Benjamin |last2=Helms |first2=Lanie |last3=Hsu |first3=Juliana |last4=Johnson |first4=Kent |last5=Shang |first5=Stephanie |last6=Wood |first6=Cal |title=The Giants of the Nuclear Testing Era: A Series of Notebooks from the Pioneers: The Works of Dr. Seymour Sack |publisher=Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory |location=Livermore, California |year=2018 |id=LLNL-MI-768642 |url=https://sd.llnl.gov/sites/sd/files/2022-03/Giants-Notebook_Seymour-Sack_Spread-mobile.pdf |access-date=2026-05-10}}</ref> Sack completed a Ph.D. dissertation at Yale University in 1954 titled ''Theory Of Low Energy Proton-alpha And Neutron-alpha Scattering''.<ref name="Sack1954">{{cite thesis |last=Sack |first=Seymour |title=Theory Of Low Energy Proton-alpha And Neutron-alpha Scattering |type=Ph.D. dissertation |publisher=Yale University |location=New Haven, Connecticut |year=1954 |url=https://search.library.yale.edu/catalog/99149640113408651 |access-date=2026-05-10}}</ref>

==Career==
Sack joined Livermore Radiation Laboratory, later renamed as [[Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory]], in 1955 to focus on calculations of two-dimensional [[fluid dynamics]], [[compressible flow]]s, and shock phenomena.<ref name="Lucchetti2011" /><ref name="Grover2018" /> He first worked in the Theoretical Physics Division, and then he joined the B Division (small weapons) in 1964.<ref name="Lucchetti2011" /><ref name="Grover2018" /> Early in his career, he worked on the trigger or 'primary' of the weapons, and later he was a project manager and designer for several warheads.<ref name="Grover2018" />  Sack retired from LLNL in 1990, but he continued to work as a laboratory associate; he remained active in weapons design, policy, and mentoring.<ref name="Lucchetti2011" /><ref name="Grover2018" /> 

In 1995, Sack was one of several nuclear weapon designers on an independent [[JASON (advisory group)|JASON]] study on nuclear testing chaired by [[Sidney Drell]].<ref name="Brown2019">{{cite report |last=Brown |first=Paul |title=The Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty: Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory's Impact on U.S. Nuclear Policy from 1958 to 2000 |publisher=Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory Office of Defense Coordination |date=2019-04-01 |url=https://cgsr.llnl.gov/sites/cgsr/files/2024-08/Brown-CTBTbook.pdf |access-date=2026-05-10}}</ref> Sack participated in the study in his capacity as an LLNL nuclear weapon primary-stage designer and as project manager for the [[B83 nuclear bomb]] and [[W84]] warheads.<ref name="Brown2019" /> The JASON study considered and contributed work towards the [[Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty]] and stockpile planning.<ref name="Brown2019" /> This was part of Sack's work on robustness in nuclear weapons design (i.e. the capability of a weapon to function reliably as designed, even under extreme environments), a topic on which he wrote internal articles.<ref name="Grover2018" /> Sack's ideas contributed to the formulation of the [[quantification of margins and uncertainties]] (QMU) at LLNL.<ref name="Grover2018" /> After retirement, Sack wrote about his opposition to renewed nuclear testing, based on technical grounds.<ref name="Sack2000">{{cite news |last=Sack |first=Seymour |title=Maintaining Nuclear Weapons |newspaper=The New York Times |date=2000-12-05 |type=Letter to the editor |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2000/12/05/science/l-maintaining-nuclear-weapons-531570.html |access-date=2026-05-10}}</ref> Sack was recorded in videos for the preservation of his nuclear weapons knowledge, focusing on weapon models and explanations of design history.<ref name="Stober1999">{{cite journal |last=Stober |first=Dan |title=Nuclear secrets: Steal this! |journal=Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists |year=1999 |volume=55 |issue=4 |pages=14–16 |doi=10.2968/055004005 |url=https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/pdf/10.2968/055004005|doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Nuclear weapons design==
A focus of Sack's work was on the development of nuclear warheads that were safer to work with and around. He developed two-dimensional hydrodynamic codes to simulate the implosion process of nuclear devices, allowing for the design of more reliable and modern warheads.<ref name="Lucchetti2011" /><ref name="Grover2018" /> In the 1960s, his design was implemented for modern primary or trigger components (the primary is the first, fission bomb component that initiates the reaction to implode and detonate the second stage, fusion); this design was deployed in the Polaris warhead for the [[W58]] primary.<ref name="Lucchetti2011" /><ref name="Grover2018" /> He also developed the use of [[Insensitive munition|Insensitive High Explosives]] (IHE) and fire-resistant plutonium pits, reducing risks in crash and fire accident scenarios, including nuclear detonation.<ref name="Grover2018" /> Even later, he worked on the [[B83 nuclear bomb|B83]], [[W84]], and [[W87]] programs, and with the W87, his design implemented multiple safety innovations in a strategic missile warhead.<ref name="Lucchetti2011" /><ref name="Grover2018" />

Among other safety innovations that Sack worked on, he directed integration of [[TATB]] into a nuclear weapon design in 1974, with his designs enabling the reliable use of TATB in nuclear weapons.<ref name="Grover2018" />

Sack also designed primaries for "miniature" bombs in the [[UGM-73 Poseidon|Poseidon submarine-launched ballistic missile]] and the [[LGM-30 Minuteman|Minuteman intercontinental ballistic missile]], including work associated with the [[W62]]/Mk12 and [[W68]]/Mk3 programs.<ref name="Lucchetti2011" /><ref name="Grover2018" /> He later worked on safer air-carried and ground-launched cruise missile weapons, including the B83 and W84 programs.<ref name="Grover2018" />

==Awards and honors==
Sack received the Ernest Orlando Lawrence Award in 1973 for his contributions to nuclear weapons theory, computer codes, design concepts, and stockpile engineering and testing.<ref name="DOE1973">{{cite web |title=Seymour Sack, 1973 |website=U.S. Department of Energy Office of Science |url=https://science.osti.gov/lawrence/Award-Laureates/1970s/sack |access-date=2026-05-10}}</ref><ref name="Lucchetti2011" /> He received the Fleet Ballistic Missile Achievement Award in 1997 for work associated with [[W62]] and [[W68]] nuclear warheads, and the Y-12 Award of Excellence in 1990.<ref name="Lucchetti2011" /><ref name="Grover2018" /> Sack's received the presidential [[Enrico Fermi Award]] in 2003 for his career's work on nuclear weapons reliability and deterrence.<ref name="Lucchetti2011" /><ref name="Grover2018" /><ref name="DOE2003">{{cite web |title=The Enrico Fermi Award; Seymour Sack, 2003 |website=U.S. Department of Energy Office of Science |date=2016-03-05 |url=https://science.osti.gov/fermi/Award-Laureates/2000s/sack |access-date=2026-05-10}}</ref>
